reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A benign autosomal recessive disorder requiring loss of function of both hepatic uptake transporters OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 (genes SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3)
It causes chronic, predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normal liver enzymes and normal synthetic function
Unlike Dubin-Johnson syndrome, the liver is histologically normal and not pigmented
Total urinary coproporphyrin is markedly elevated, with a relatively increased coproporphyrin I fraction, contrasting with the pattern in Dubin-Johnson syndrome
Hepatobiliary scintigraphy typically shows poor or absent hepatic uptake, whereas gallbladder visualisation is generally preserved
The defect impairs hepatic re-uptake of conjugated bilirubin that has undergone physiological hepatocyte efflux, so it accumulates in plasma
No treatment is needed as the condition is entirely benign with normal longevity
reference.pathophysiology: The organic anion transporting polypeptides OATP1B1 and OATP1B3, encoded by SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3 on the sinusoidal (basolateral) hepatocyte membrane, mediate uptake of bilirubin and other organic anions from blood into the liver. A portion of conjugated bilirubin normally effluxes from hepatocytes back into the sinusoids and is then re-taken up by these transporters. In Rotor syndrome, combined deficiency of both transporters abolishes this reuptake, so conjugated bilirubin accumulates in the circulation, producing conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Because the canalicular excretory machinery and hepatocyte architecture are intact, the liver appears normal without the pigment seen in Dubin-Johnson syndrome.
additionalInvestigations: Fractionated bilirubin confirming a conjugated predominance
Normal liver enzymes and synthetic function excluding hepatocellular or obstructive disease
Total and fractionated urinary coproporphyrin showing markedly raised total excretion
Hepatobiliary scintigraphy demonstrating impaired hepatic uptake
Liver biopsy (if performed) showing normal, non-pigmented histology
SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3 molecular genetic testing where confirmation is needed
redFlags: Abnormal transaminases or impaired synthetic function suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Clinical signs of true biliary obstruction such as pale stools and pruritus
Systemic or constitutional symptoms prompting exclusion of serious hepatobiliary disease
Altered handling of drugs that rely on OATP transporters, raising toxicity risk
reference.prognosis: Rotor syndrome is benign with a normal life expectancy and no progression to chronic liver disease; recognition mainly serves to avoid unnecessary investigation and to anticipate altered disposition of OATP-dependent drugs.
pitfalls: Confusing Rotor with Dubin-Johnson syndrome despite their differing pigment and coproporphyrin patterns
Pursuing invasive workup for a benign conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
Failing to anticipate altered pharmacokinetics of drugs transported by OATP1B1/1B3, such as certain statins
Overlooking the requirement for biallelic loss of both transporters when interpreting genetics
Attributing the jaundice to hepatocellular disease despite normal liver enzymes
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
management: Reassurance and patient education about the benign nature and normal life expectancy, with no specific treatment required
Avoidance of unnecessary invasive investigation for the isolated conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia once the diagnosis is established
Anticipating and adjusting for altered disposition of OATP1B1/OATP1B3-dependent drugs such as statins, methotrexate and certain antibiotics to prevent toxicity
Recognition that jaundice may fluctuate or worsen with intercurrent illness yet requires no intervention
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance requiring biallelic SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3 defects, with family clarification as needed
